content:
GreenCart GmbH runs a subscription grocery-delivery service in Germany. Sofia signs up online for a weekly “family box.” During checkout, GreenCart collects her name, delivery address, email, phone number, chosen delivery slot, and subscription plan. It also stores an order history so Sofia can manage pauses and refunds under the subscription terms. To take payment, GreenCart sends Sofia’s card details to a payment service provider, which returns a payment token; GreenCart stores only the token and transaction reference to charge recurring payments and handle chargebacks.

To deliver the box, GreenCart shares Sofia’s name, address, phone number, and delivery instructions with its contracted courier, and sends SMS delivery notifications. Separately, GreenCart retains invoice data (name, address, items, VAT, invoice number, and payment references) for 10 years to comply with German tax/accounting retention requirements, and restricts access to the finance team.

GreenCart also offers an optional “Dietary preferences” field. Sofia enters “severe nut allergy.” GreenCart uses this information to filter products and display allergy warnings in her account. The field is marked optional and can be left blank; core ordering and delivery still work without it.

Yes/No Question:
Is GreenCart’s processing of (i) account, delivery, and payment-token data, (ii) invoice retention data, and (iii) the optional nut-allergy preference lawful under GDPR Article 6 (i.e., does at least one legal basis in Art. 6(1)(a)-(f) apply to each purpose)?

A mid-sized EU online pharmacy, MediCart GmbH (based in Munich), sells prescription refills and over-the-counter products through its website and mobile app. A customer, Sofia, creates an account to order a recurring 30‑day refill for hypertension medication. During checkout, MediCart collects Sofia’s name, delivery address, date of birth (to verify age and match prescriptions), prescription ID, medication details, payment card token (stored by a payment processor), and contact information.  

To reduce fraud and failed deliveries, MediCart also runs an automated “address and identity verification” step. It sends Sofia’s name, address, date of birth, device ID, IP address, and order history to a third‑party verification vendor. The vendor returns a risk score and a “verified/not verified” result that MediCart stores for 18 months. This verification runs by default for all orders above €50, including recurring refills, and Sofia cannot opt out without canceling the purchase. MediCart’s privacy notice states that verification is used to “secure transactions and prevent misuse,” but it does not request explicit consent for this vendor sharing.  

MediCart argues it must perform verification to safely deliver controlled medicines and prevent chargebacks, and that processing is necessary to fulfill the customer’s order. Sofia complains that sharing her data with the vendor is excessive and not required for delivering the medication.

Yes/No Question:  
Under GDPR Article 6, is MediCart’s sharing of Sofia’s data with the verification vendor lawful without her explicit consent because it is necessary for contract performance or legitimate interests?

A UK-based online pharmacy, MedCart Ltd., sells over-the-counter allergy medicines through its website to EU customers. Sofia (in Spain) places an order for antihistamine tablets and requests home delivery. To process the purchase, MedCart collects Sofia’s name, delivery address, email, phone number, items ordered, delivery instructions, and payment token. It sends the payment token and order amount to a payment service provider to charge her card and sends her name, address, and phone number to a courier to deliver the parcel. MedCart stores order confirmations and invoices for 7 years to comply with UK tax/accounting recordkeeping obligations and to respond to possible chargebacks.

Separately, MedCart runs basic fraud-prevention: it logs Sofia’s IP address, device ID, and attempted payment history, and uses a rules-based tool to flag unusually high quantities or repeated failed payments. Flagged orders are reviewed by staff; if the order is blocked, Sofia is notified and can contact support. MedCart documents a legitimate-interests assessment concluding the fraud checks are necessary to protect its and the payment provider’s interests, limited to what is needed, retained for 90 days, and unlikely to override Sofia’s rights given transparency, opt-out where feasible, and minimal impact.

MedCart does not use Sofia’s data for marketing unless she separately ticks an optional consent box.

Yes/No Question:
Is MedCart’s processing of Sofia’s personal data lawful under GDPR Article 6 because at least one lawful basis applies to each processing purpose (contract performance, legal obligation, or legitimate interests after balancing)?

A Germany-based online pharmacy (“MediShip GmbH”) offers a monthly home-delivery subscription for repeat prescriptions (e.g., asthma inhalers). Customers create an account and upload an ePrescription token or a scanned prescription. MediShip processes: identity and contact details, delivery address, date of birth (to verify eligibility), prescription details (medicine name, dosage, prescribing doctor, refill quantity), payment data (SEPA mandate or card token), and order history. The pharmacy transmits necessary prescription and delivery data to (i) a licensed partner wholesaler for fulfillment, (ii) a payment service provider to charge the monthly fee, and (iii) a parcel carrier for delivery tracking. 

MediShip retains dispensing records, pharmacist verification logs, and invoice data for 10 years to meet pharmacy, tax, and medicines-traceability obligations under German law and EU rules. It also runs automated checks to detect duplicate prescriptions and suspicious ordering patterns to prevent fraud and ensure patient safety. Optional fields (phone number) are used only for delivery issues; marketing emails are sent only if the customer opts in. MediShip does not rely on “legitimate interests” for core dispensing because it is a regulated activity; instead it maps each purpose to a legal basis (contract performance for subscription fulfillment and payment; legal obligation for mandatory record-keeping and regulatory reporting). Prescription data is treated as health data and handled with restricted access.

Yes/No Question:
Is MediShip’s processing of customer account, payment, and prescription/dispensing data lawful under GDPR Article 6 because at least one legal basis (e.g., contract necessity and/or legal obligation) applies to each processing purpose?

A Berlin-based meal-kit company, FreshBox GmbH, runs an online subscription service. A customer, Lara, selects a weekly plan and enters her name, delivery address, phone number, and preferred delivery window. FreshBox uses these details to confirm the order, assign a courier, send delivery updates by SMS, and handle customer support tickets. FreshBox stores invoices and payment confirmations for 10 years to meet German tax/accounting retention rules.  

During checkout, FreshBox shows an optional section titled “Allergies/medical dietary needs (optional).” The page explains: “If you provide allergy or medical dietary information, we will use it to tailor ingredient substitutions and to flag allergens on packing labels.” Lara types “celiac disease (gluten-free)” and submits the order. The checkbox next to this field says: “I explicitly consent to FreshBox processing my health-related information for dietary customization,” with a link to a privacy notice describing purposes, retention (deleted after 6 months), and withdrawal (via account settings). The allergy data is stored in a separate database table with restricted staff access, and is shared only with the contracted packaging partner for label printing.  

FreshBox also logs IP address, device ID, and failed payment attempts to detect fraud and account takeover; these logs are retained for 30 days and are not used for marketing.

Yes/No Question:  
For each purpose described (order fulfillment, invoice retention, dietary customization using health data, and fraud prevention), does FreshBox have at least one lawful basis under GDPR Article 6 to process Lara’s personal data?

A mid-sized online pharmacy in Germany, “MediDirect GmbH,” sells prescription and over‑the‑counter medicines through its website and app. A customer, Anna, creates an account and orders a prescription asthma inhaler. To fulfill the order, MediDirect collects and processes her name, delivery address, date of birth (to verify age), prescription details, and payment information. The company also stores order history in her account so she can track shipments and request refills.

MediDirect contracts with a logistics provider to deliver parcels and shares Anna’s name, address, and phone number for delivery notifications. The pharmacy’s payment processor receives Anna’s card details and billing address. Separately, MediDirect retains invoice and transaction records (including Anna’s name, address, items purchased, and totals) for 10 years to comply with German tax and accounting retention requirements. Access to prescription data is restricted to licensed pharmacists, and all data transfers to processors are covered by written data processing agreements.

Anna later contacts support and says she never explicitly checked a box consenting to “data processing,” and she requests deletion of all her data immediately, including prescription and invoice records. MediDirect explains that it cannot delete certain records because they are needed to complete the sale and to meet statutory retention obligations, but it can delete optional marketing preferences (she is not subscribed to marketing).

Yes/No Question:  
Is MediDirect’s processing of Anna’s personal data for order fulfillment and legally required record retention lawful under GDPR Article 6 even without explicit consent?

A mid-sized logistics company in Germany (“NordHaul GmbH,” 650 employees) introduces a new “Fit-to-Work” program to reduce accidents in its warehouse. The company contracts an occupational health provider to perform annual medical checks for forklift operators and night-shift staff. During the check, the provider collects employees’ blood pressure, medication list, sleep disorder indicators, and results from a drug screening panel. The provider also takes a fingerprint scan to verify that the right employee is attending the appointment and to prevent identity fraud. These results are uploaded to NordHaul’s HR portal.

NordHaul’s HR team can view detailed test results and is instructed to flag employees as “cleared,” “restricted duties,” or “unfit,” and to schedule follow-up appointments. The company keeps the full medical reports for five years “in case of future claims.” Employees are told the checks are mandatory; refusing may lead to reassignment. The only notice provided is a short email stating the program is “for safety,” without mentioning GDPR Article 9 data, legal basis, or who will access the data. No explicit consent is collected. The company’s works council was informed but did not approve specific data access controls. The occupational health provider is paid per report and has no separate system for storing data outside NordHaul’s portal.

Yes/No Question:  
Under GDPR Article 9, is NordHaul allowed to process and store employees’ detailed medical and biometric (fingerprint) data in its HR portal without explicit consent, relying solely on workplace safety needs?

A mid-sized logistics company in Germany (“NordShip GmbH,” 1,200 employees) introduces a new “SafeLift” program to reduce warehouse injuries. HR contracts an occupational health clinic to run voluntary medical screenings at two distribution centers. During the screening, the clinic collects employees’ blood pressure, past musculoskeletal injuries, medication use, and doctor notes about fitness to perform heavy lifting (health data). To prevent “buddy punching,” NordShip also replaces badge swipes with fingerprint scanners at the warehouse entrances (biometric data used for identification).

The clinic sends NordShip a monthly spreadsheet listing each screened employee by name, their detailed medical findings, and a recommended work restriction (e.g., “no lifting over 15kg for 6 weeks”). NordShip uploads the spreadsheet into its HR system, where line managers can view it to plan shifts. Separately, the fingerprint templates are stored by NordShip’s security vendor in a cloud database and retained for five years after employment ends. Employees are told participation in the medical screening is “voluntary,” but managers strongly encourage it and suggest it will be considered in performance reviews. The company has not obtained explicit consent for either the medical data transfer to managers or the fingerprint system; it relies on “workplace safety” and “efficiency.” No data protection impact assessment has been completed.

Yes/No Question:  
Under GDPR Article 9, is NordShip allowed to process and share these employees’ health details and fingerprint-based biometric identifiers without explicit consent, based solely on general workplace safety and efficiency reasons?

A German automotive parts manufacturer (“AutoForge GmbH”) runs a mandatory “fit-for-work” program for employees assigned to high-risk chemical handling. Before being scheduled, each employee must complete an online medical questionnaire hosted by a cloud HR vendor. The questionnaire asks about chronic illnesses (e.g., asthma), current medications, past mental-health treatment, pregnancy status, and recent sick leave patterns. Employees must also upload a physician-issued “fitness certificate” stating whether they are fit, fit with restrictions, or unfit for specific tasks. The HR vendor stores the full questionnaire and certificate in the EU for 24 months and provides dashboards to AutoForge’s HR team and line managers.

AutoForge wants to use the detailed answers to: (1) decide who can work in solvent areas, (2) set individual shift limits, and (3) flag employees for follow-up interviews. Line managers can see the underlying diagnoses and medications in the dashboard. Participation is compulsory; refusing the questionnaire leads to removal from the role. AutoForge does not cite a specific German legal provision authorizing HR to view diagnostic details, and the processing is not limited to an occupational physician. No explicit, separate consent is collected beyond a general “I acknowledge” checkbox.

Yes/No Question:
Is AutoForge allowed under GDPR Article 9 to process these health and mental-health data as described (including HR/manager access to diagnoses) without a valid Article 9(2) exception such as occupational medicine safeguards or explicit, freely given consent?

A mid-sized logistics company in Germany (“NordRoute GmbH”) runs a warehouse with 420 employees and uses a third-party time-and-attendance system. After several minor accidents, management decides to introduce an “enhanced safety access” program for forklift operators. Operators must pass a fitness-for-work check and then use a fingerprint scanner at the forklift bay to unlock and start vehicles. The vendor stores fingerprint templates in its cloud and links them to each employee’s ID, shift records, and accident history. HR also uploads the occupational physician’s “fit/unfit” assessment and notes about conditions such as epilepsy, diabetes, and sleep apnea to the same platform so supervisors can reassign tasks.

NordRoute tells staff the program is “mandatory for safety and insurance.” Employees receive a short notice in the onboarding portal, but no separate explicit consent form. The works council was informed, but no formal agreement is signed. Access to the health notes is given to HR, the safety officer, and all shift supervisors. The company retains the biometric templates and health assessments for five years, including for employees who stop operating forklifts. The vendor may use aggregated data to “improve authentication accuracy,” and NordRoute has not documented an alternative (e.g., badge + PIN) for those who refuse fingerprint scanning.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 9, is NordRoute allowed to process forklift operators’ biometric data and health information in this way without obtaining explicit consent?

MedWerk GmbH (a 1,200-employee manufacturing company in Germany) introduces an annual “Fit for Work” medical screening program. Employees book appointments through an internal HR portal that requires selecting one or more “reasons for screening” from a dropdown (e.g., “blood pressure issues,” “diabetes monitoring,” “fertility treatment,” “mental health counseling,” “suspected sleep apnea”). The portal also asks for current medications and allergies “to help the doctor prepare.”

Appointments are carried out by an external occupational health provider (Arbeitsmedizinisches Zentrum GmbH). The provider’s doctors are subject to professional secrecy. However, the booking portal is operated by MedWerk HR, and HR staff can access each employee’s booking record, including the selected reasons, medications, and allergies, to “manage capacity and follow up on no-shows.” HR exports monthly reports listing employee names and selected reasons to plant management to “plan staffing risks.” Participation is described as “voluntary,” but managers repeatedly encourage enrollment and employees who do not participate are asked to explain why during performance check-ins. Employees are shown a consent checkbox in the portal stating: “I agree to processing of my health data for the screening program,” with no separate option to book without providing reasons/medications.

MedWerk relies on (i) employee consent and (ii) occupational health purposes to justify processing.

Yes/No Question:
Does GDPR Article 9 allow MedWerk to process these health details in an HR-run portal and share aggregated-by-name “reasons for screening” with management under an Article 9(2) exception (e.g., explicit consent or occupational/preventive medicine), assuming an Article 6 basis is also identified?

A startup called **DermaNow** offers teledermatology in Germany. Users create an account, then upload **close-up photos of a mole or rash** and complete a **symptom questionnaire** (itching, pain, fever, medications, pregnancy status). The app automatically tags images with date/time and device ID. DermaNow uses an AI triage model to prioritize urgent cases, then a **licensed dermatologist** reviews the case and sends a diagnosis and treatment plan. DermaNow stores the case file in its cloud database for 12 months for follow-up and billing.

DermaNow also offers an optional **“Face Unlock”** login: the app scans the user’s face and generates a template used **to uniquely authenticate** the user on subsequent logins. This biometric feature is presented as optional and has a separate consent screen labeled “Explicit consent to biometric processing for authentication,” with a toggle and a “withdraw anytime” button. If a user withdraws, Face Unlock is disabled and the template is deleted.

DermaNow’s platform engineers can access production logs for debugging; logs may include user IDs and file names. Dermatologists are bound by medical confidentiality; DermaNow signs contracts requiring all staff with access to health cases to follow confidentiality and limits access via role-based controls.

Yes/No Question:
**Is DermaNow allowed under GDPR Article 9 to process users’ health data (photos + symptom questionnaire) and biometric Face Unlock templates for these purposes?**

A German chemical manufacturing company, RheinChem GmbH, operates a high-hazard plant where only specially trained staff may enter the chlorine storage and mixing areas. To prevent unauthorized entry and to meet workplace safety and incident-traceability requirements, RheinChem introduces biometric access control at three “restricted zones.” Employees and long-term on-site contractors must enroll a fingerprint, which is converted into a mathematical template (not stored as an image). The templates are encrypted at rest, stored on an EU-based access-control server, and linked to an employee ID. Access logs (template ID, door, timestamp, success/fail) are retained for 12 months for safety investigations; templates are deleted within 30 days after termination.

RheinChem states the system is “necessary” because badges can be shared and PINs can be observed. As an alternative, it considered photo badges plus guards but rejected them as “too costly.” Enrollment is presented as mandatory for restricted-zone workers; no comparable non-biometric option is offered. RheinChem provides a privacy notice and role-based access to the system, but it does not cite a specific German law that explicitly authorizes biometric identification for this purpose, beyond general occupational safety duties. No explicit written consent is collected, and refusal may lead to reassignment away from restricted zones.

Yes/No Question:
Is RheinChem allowed under GDPR Article 9 to process fingerprint templates for uniquely identifying workers to control access to restricted zones in this scenario?

A logistics company, NorthDock Warehousing GmbH (Germany), is hiring forklift operators. Applicants apply via an online portal run by a vendor, SkillGate. During the application, SkillGate requires: (1) a “fitness-to-work” questionnaire asking about epilepsy, diabetes, heart conditions, current medications, past depression/anxiety treatment, and any work-related injuries (health data); and (2) a short selfie video that SkillGate’s software analyzes to “verify identity and prevent fraud” by creating a facial template and matching it to the applicant’s ID photo (biometric data used for unique identification).

NorthDock says the purpose is to ensure operators can safely perform safety-critical tasks and to comply with workplace safety obligations. The portal states that completion is “mandatory to proceed.” It does not offer an alternative, such as an in-person occupational health assessment. The privacy notice cites “legitimate interests” and “safety” but does not reference any specific German/EU employment or occupational-health law authorizing this processing. No explicit consent checkbox is provided; applicants can only click “Submit application.”

SkillGate stores the questionnaire responses and facial template for 24 months to “improve screening models” and allows NorthDock to download a risk score (fit/unfit) plus flagged conditions. No health professional is involved, and there is no mention of confidentiality obligations comparable to medical secrecy. Applicants are not told that biometric templates are retained separately from the video.

Yes/No Question:
Is NorthDock/SkillGate allowed under GDPR Article 9 to process applicants’ health data and biometric facial templates in this way without obtaining explicit consent or relying on a clearly identified employment/occupational-medicine legal basis with required safeguards?

NordLift GmbH is a logistics company in Hamburg with 180 employees. To reduce accidents, it requires all warehouse staff who operate forklifts to complete an annual “fitness-to-drive” assessment. The assessment is conducted by an external occupational health clinic during paid working hours. Employees must complete a medical questionnaire (epilepsy history, diabetes, sleep disorders, medications, vision issues, past workplace injuries) and undergo a brief examination and reaction-time test. The clinic records the results in its medical system and sends NordLift a standardized certificate with one of three outcomes: “fit,” “fit with restrictions” (e.g., no night shifts, must wear corrective lenses), or “temporarily unfit—review in 3 months.” 

NordLift’s HR department stores the certificates in a restricted digital folder for five years and logs any work restrictions in the scheduling tool so supervisors can assign duties accordingly. Managers are instructed not to request diagnoses, but in practice some supervisors ask employees why they were marked “unfit.” NordLift does not obtain explicit consent, arguing the checks are necessary for workplace safety and to comply with occupational health and safety obligations. Employees who refuse the assessment are removed from forklift duties and may lose shift premiums.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 9, may NordLift process these health assessment results (special category health data) without explicit consent because the processing is necessary for occupational medicine/workplace safety purposes?

NorthBridge Rail GmbH operates freight trains in Germany and Poland. For safety‑critical roles (locomotive drivers and shunters), it must ensure employees are medically fit for duty under national rail safety and occupational health rules that require periodic occupational health assessments by an accredited occupational physician and impose medical confidentiality obligations.

NorthBridge contracts “FitWork Occupational Health,” a clinic staffed by licensed physicians. FitWork collects special category data: blood pressure, vision/hearing test results, medication lists, and a brief mental‑health screening questionnaire for fatigue and substance‑dependency risk. Employees book appointments through a vendor portal (“ShiftHR”), which only receives appointment slots and employee IDs.

FitWork conducts the exam and stores detailed medical records in its own system. FitWork sends NorthBridge only a fitness certificate with one of three outcomes: “fit,” “fit with restrictions” (e.g., no night shifts for 3 months), or “temporarily unfit,” plus an expiry date. No diagnoses are shared. NorthBridge HR stores the certificate in a restricted-access folder and uses it solely to assign shifts and comply with safety audits. Access is limited to two HR specialists and the safety manager; line managers see only work restrictions. Certificates are retained for 5 years to match statutory limitation/audit periods. Employees are told the assessment is mandatory for these roles; NorthBridge does not rely on consent.

Yes/No Question:
Is NorthBridge’s processing of employees’ health data lawful under GDPR Article 9 (e.g., as necessary for employment/social-security obligations or occupational medicine/fitness-for-work, with required legal authorisation and safeguards)?

Lina (32) uses “PulsePath,” an EU-based fitness and navigation app with a paid subscription. To run the service, PulsePath processes her account data (email, password hash, billing address, subscription status) under the contract. Separately, Lina opted in (via a toggle) to two optional features based on consent: (1) collecting continuous heart-rate and sleep data from her wearable for “wellness insights,” and (2) collecting precise GPS location in the background to generate “training heatmaps.” The app privacy notice states these optional datasets are also used for personalized ads.

After six months, Lina cancels her subscription and withdraws both consents in the app settings. She also submits an Article 21 objection to any processing for direct marketing, including the use of her hashed email for “lookalike audiences” shared with an ad platform. PulsePath confirms the cancellation but replies it will keep all data for five years “for analytics and improvement,” and will retain transaction records for tax law. Lina points out she no longer uses the service, wants her wearable metrics, heatmaps, and ad identifiers erased, and asks that any recipients be informed. PulsePath does not claim any need to keep the health/location data for legal claims, research archiving, or freedom of expression.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 17, must PulsePath erase Lina’s consent-based wearable health data, precise location history/heatmaps, and ad identifiers (while possibly retaining only what is necessary for tax/legal obligations)?

FitTrack Jr. is an EU-based fitness app offering family accounts. Lara (34) created an account to manage her son Tim’s (12) smartwatch. During sign-up, the app asked for Tim’s date of birth (showing he is 12), heart-rate data, sleep patterns, and GPS routes “to provide activity reports and safety alerts.” The privacy settings screen had one “Agree” button covering (a) core app operation, (b) personalised ads, and (c) sharing “wellness insights” with “research and commercial partners.” No separate opt-in was shown for health data sharing or marketing, and Tim could not use the watch without pressing “Agree.”

After six months, Lara disables location tracking and cancels the subscription. She then objects (Art. 21) to any direct marketing and asks FitTrack Jr. to delete Tim’s profile and all historical heart-rate, sleep, and location data. FitTrack Jr. stops marketing emails but refuses deletion, saying it has “legitimate interests” to keep the data to “improve algorithms,” and notes some data was exported to two analytics partners. It also says it must retain invoices and payment records for 7 years under national tax law, and keep minimal logs for potential disputes about an allegedly defective device.

Lara repeats the request and asks FitTrack Jr. to inform the partners to erase the data too.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 17, must FitTrack Jr. erase Tim’s personal data (and take reasonable steps to notify the partners), except for any portions it must retain for legal obligations or legal claims?

BrightSteps GmbH runs a paid fitness app in Germany. Users create an account (name, email, password hash, billing address) and optionally enter health-related data (weight, injuries, heart-rate from a wearable) to receive personalized training plans. BrightSteps also uses a “marketing audiences” feature: it uploads a hashed version of users’ emails to AdCloud Ltd. to run targeted ads and create lookalike audiences.

Mara (16) signed up two years ago using her own email and entered optional injury notes and heart-rate data. She cancels her subscription and deletes the app account. On the same day she sends a written request to BrightSteps to “delete everything about me,” and specifically withdraws her consent for personalization and for any sharing with advertising partners. She also objects to any direct marketing.

BrightSteps stops sending marketing emails. However, it keeps (1) Mara’s full account profile and training history “in case she returns,” (2) the hashed email identifier stored in its marketing-audience list and does not notify AdCloud to remove it, and (3) invoice records for the subscription, stating it must retain them for tax law. BrightSteps has no ongoing dispute with Mara, but its support team notes that chargebacks are possible for 6 months after cancellation.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 17, must BrightSteps erase Mara’s personal data (including marketing identifiers) and take reasonable steps to inform AdCloud to erase it, except for any data it must retain by law (e.g., invoices)?

FreshFork GmbH runs a meal-kit app in Germany. Lena (16) created an account to receive weekly deliveries and paid by card. During sign-up she entered her name, address, email, phone number, and date of birth. She also optionally filled in a “Health & Diet” profile (allergies: peanuts; medical note: celiac disease) to filter recipes; FreshFork states this profile is processed based on explicit consent and can be deleted at any time. FreshFork processes order history, delivery logs, customer-service chats, and payment/invoice records mainly to perform the subscription contract and meet tax/accounting retention duties.

After three months Lena cancels the subscription and withdraws her consent for the Health & Diet profile. She also objects (Art. 21) to her data being used for personalized marketing and asks FreshFork to delete “everything.” FreshFork stops marketing and deletes her Health & Diet profile, but refuses to erase invoices, payment transaction references, and delivery records, citing legal obligations and the need to defend against potential chargebacks. FreshFork also tells Lena it had shared her profile with a recipe-personalization vendor; FreshFork sends the vendor an erasure request and asks them to delete links or copies where feasible.

Lena insists that because she is 16 and the app is an information society service, all her data must be erased immediately, including invoices and order history.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 17, must FreshFork erase all of Lena’s personal data (including invoices and order history), rather than only deleting the consent-based health profile and ceasing marketing while retaining legally required records?

A customer, Sofia Marin, has used “MoveFast,” a ride-hailing app operating in Spain, for two years. The service is provided by MoveFast Mobility S.L., which acts as the controller. Sofia paid with a saved Visa card, enabled location services, and occasionally contacted in-app support about fare disputes. MoveFast’s privacy notice says it processes personal data to provide rides, prevent fraud, improve service, and send marketing offers (unless opted out). Data collected includes account details (name, email, phone), trip history (pickup/drop-off points, timestamps, route GPS traces), device identifiers, payment tokens from a payment processor, customer support chat transcripts, and ratings she gave drivers.

After a recent news article about location tracking, Sofia emails MoveFast’s privacy address requesting: (1) confirmation whether her personal data is being processed; (2) a copy of all personal data held about her; (3) the purposes of processing; (4) categories of personal data; (5) recipients or categories of recipients (e.g., drivers, analytics providers, payment processor); (6) the retention period for trip GPS logs and support chats; and (7) information about her rights to rectification, erasure, restriction, objection, and lodging a complaint. She asks that the response be provided in a readable electronic format.

MoveFast acknowledges receipt but says it will only provide a “summary” of her last 10 rides and refuses to disclose recipients, claiming it is “confidential business information,” and indicates it may take “up to three months” due to workload.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 15, must MoveFast provide Sofia confirmation and access to her personal data (including purposes, categories, recipients, and retention information) in a transparent form within one month?

PulseFit is a EU-based fitness app. In its privacy notice, PulseFit says it processes users’ in-app activity (workout frequency, completed plans, time of day, device type) and location at city level to create “engagement segments” (e.g., “likely to churn,” “power users”). The company relies on **legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f))** to (1) analyze usage trends and (2) run **targeted promotional campaigns**. Each week, PulseFit uses these segments to send tailored **email and push notifications** promoting paid subscriptions and partner products (sportswear discounts). This targeting includes profiling: users who miss two workouts receive “Come back—50% off Premium” offers, while frequent users get bundle offers.

Marta, a free-tier user in Spain, finds the targeting intrusive. She emails support: “I object to you profiling me and using my activity data to send targeted promotions. Stop processing my data for marketing.” She also adds: “I object to processing based on your ‘legitimate interests’ for segmentation.” PulseFit replies that segmentation is essential for business growth and will continue, but offers Marta an option to “mute promotional notifications for 30 days.” The marketing emails keep coming.

PulseFit’s in-app account settings do not mention a right to object, and the marketing emails do not include a clear, separate notice that she can object to direct marketing.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 21, must PulseFit stop processing Marta’s data for profiling/segmentation **used for direct marketing** after her objection?

A mid-sized online electronics retailer, BrightCart GmbH, operates in Germany and sells through its website and mobile app. When customers create an account, BrightCart collects identity and contact data (name, email, phone), purchase history, browsing events (pages viewed, time spent, cart additions), and device identifiers. It also buys “likely-to-upgrade” audience segments from an ad network and matches them to customer emails using a hashed identifier.

BrightCart relies on (1) consent for optional analytics cookies, but (2) “legitimate interests” to build customer profiles for “service improvement and fraud prevention,” and (3) “legitimate interests” to send promotional emails to existing customers about similar products. Marketing emails are personalized using an automated scoring model that predicts a customer’s price sensitivity and assigns them to one of three discount tiers. Customers in the “high willingness to pay” tier receive smaller discounts and see higher-priced recommendations in-app. No employee reviews these tier assignments unless a complaint is filed.

Maria, a customer, receives weekly personalized emails and notices she never gets the larger coupons her friend receives. She submits a request through BrightCart’s privacy portal stating: “I object to all processing of my data for direct marketing, including profiling related to marketing, and I object to any processing based on legitimate interests that affects the prices and offers I’m shown. I want a human to review any automated decisions that impact me.” BrightCart replies that it will keep profiling her for “legitimate interests” and will continue sending emails unless she separately unsubscribes.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 21, must BrightCart stop processing Maria’s data for direct marketing (including related profiling) upon her objection?

GreenRide, a bike‑sharing company in Berlin, uses its mobile app to rent bikes and process payments. When users create an account, GreenRide’s privacy notice says it processes location history, ride frequency, and station preferences “to improve services and prevent fraud” on the basis of **legitimate interests**. It also states users may receive “personalised offers,” but the right to object is only mentioned deep in the notice, not highlighted at first marketing contact.

After several rides, Lina starts receiving push notifications and emails promoting a new monthly subscription and partner discounts. The offers appear tailored to her commuting pattern and usual pickup stations, indicating **profiling for marketing**. Lina clicks “unsubscribe,” but the app still sends push notifications. She then emails GreenRide: (1) she **objects to processing of her data for direct marketing, including related profiling**, and (2) she **objects to continued processing of her precise location history for service‑improvement analytics** based on legitimate interests, saying it feels intrusive given her regular commute route. GreenRide replies it will “review the request,” but continues sending personalised offers and continues using her detailed location history for analytics, stating it has “strong business reasons” to keep improving station placement and retention.

Yes/No Question:  
Under GDPR Article 21, must GreenRide stop using Lina’s data for direct marketing (including related profiling) once she objects?

A mid-sized online pharmacy, MedMall, sells prescription refills and wellness products in Germany and Austria. Customers create accounts, upload prescriptions, and can opt in to a loyalty program. MedMall processes purchase history, browsing behavior on its website/app, approximate location (from IP), and inferred health interests (e.g., “allergy relief,” “diabetes care”) to build marketing segments. It relies on “legitimate interests” to send personalized discount emails and push notifications for non-prescription products, and it shares hashed email addresses with an ad platform to create “lookalike audiences.”  

After buying a glucose monitor, Lina receives frequent ads and emails about diabetes supplements. She emails MedMall: “I object to any use of my data for marketing and profiling. Stop personalized offers and stop sharing my data with ad partners.” MedMall replies that marketing is necessary to “fund the service,” offers only an “unsubscribe from emails” link, and continues push notifications. Separately, MedMall uses an automated fraud-scoring tool to decide whether to allow “pay later.” Lina is automatically denied, with a message: “Decision made automatically; no further review available.” She asks for a human review and to know what data was used. MedMall refuses, saying the model is proprietary and the decision is final.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 21, must MedMall stop processing Lina’s data for direct marketing (including related profiling and ad-platform sharing) and provide a way to object/request human intervention for the automated “pay later” decision?

MediCloud GmbH (Germany) provides a SaaS platform for physiotherapy clinics to manage appointments, treatment notes, and billing. It acts as a **processor** for 120 clinics (controllers) across the EU. The platform processes **special-category health data** (diagnoses, therapy plans, clinician notes) for ~180,000 patients and also stores contact details and insurance numbers. Data is hosted in an EU cloud region; support staff in Germany and Poland access production systems for troubleshooting.

After a DPIA and risk assessment, MediCloud documents threats (account takeover, insider access, ransomware, accidental deletion) and considers **state of the art** and **implementation costs**. Implemented measures include: TLS 1.3 in transit; AES-256 encryption at rest with customer-segregated keys in an HSM; role-based access control with least privilege; MFA for all staff; audited break-glass access; pseudonymised analytics dataset (patient IDs replaced with random tokens); centralized logging with 12‑month retention; and an incident response runbook with 24/7 on-call.

However, two gaps remain: (1) backups are taken nightly but are stored in the same cloud account and have not been tested for restoration in 9 months; the last restore drill failed due to missing IAM permissions. (2) penetration tests are ad hoc; no scheduled “regular testing” exists, and vulnerability scanning is limited to quarterly manual checks. A clinic asks MediCloud to evidence Art. 32 compliance before renewing its processing agreement.

Yes/No Question:  
Given the risk, nature, and scale of processing, does MediCloud’s current set of measures meet GDPR Article 32 requirements (including restore capability and regular testing)?

MediCall GmbH (Germany) operates a telemedicine app and web portal for 120,000 patients. It processes special-category health data (symptoms, diagnoses, prescriptions), ID data, and appointment recordings. Patients and clinicians access accounts via username/password; clinicians can also use SMS-based 2FA, but it is optional for patients. Data is stored in an EU-based cloud database; nightly backups are written to a separate EU region. A Polish IT support vendor provides 24/7 incident troubleshooting and has privileged admin access via VPN; access is shared through a single vendor account and is not limited to specific tickets. Admin actions are logged, but logs are retained only 7 days and are not reviewed unless a complaint occurs. Data at rest in the database is encrypted using provider-managed keys; exported reports (CSV) are emailed internally without encryption for billing reconciliation. The company has a written incident response plan, but the last tabletop exercise was 3 years ago, and disaster recovery restoration has never been tested end-to-end. Pseudonymisation is used for analytics, but production support often copies real patient records into a test environment to reproduce bugs. Security measures were chosen informally based on “industry practice,” without a documented assessment of likelihood/severity of risks, “state of the art” options, or implementation costs.

Yes/No Question:
Given the sensitivity, scale, and third-party privileged access, has MediCall implemented “appropriate technical and organizational measures” under GDPR Article 32 (including confidentiality/integrity/resilience, encryption/pseudonymisation where appropriate, restore capability, and regular testing/evaluation)?

BrightCart, an EU-based online retailer, maintains a customer CRM that stores order history, delivery addresses, and a “fraud risk score” used to decide whether to offer invoice payment. The score is calculated from past chargebacks and third‑party address verification results. BrightCart also keeps customer records for 5 years to handle warranty disputes.

Emma notices in her account profile that her fraud risk score is marked “high” and shows an old address in another city. Because of this, BrightCart blocks invoice payment and flags her new orders for manual review, delaying shipment. Emma emails BrightCart stating the address and score are inaccurate: she never lived at that address and has never had a chargeback. She provides proof of her current address and asks BrightCart to “freeze” any use of the fraud score and stop automated decision-making based on it until the company verifies and corrects the data.

BrightCart replies that it will investigate with the address-verification vendor, which may take up to 14 days, and continues using the existing fraud score to restrict Emma’s payment options during the investigation. Emma reiterates that she is contesting the accuracy of the data and requests restriction of processing of the disputed fields (old address and fraud score) while verification is pending.

Yes/No Question:  
Under GDPR Article 18(1)(a), must BrightCart restrict processing of Emma’s disputed address and fraud risk score while it verifies their accuracy?

Marta, a customer in Spain, uses “PayWave,” a mobile payments app. PayWave profiles transactions to detect fraud and reduce chargebacks, relying on Art. 6(1)(f) (legitimate interests). It stores: Marta’s name, account ID, device ID, IP addresses, geolocation at time of payment, transaction history, and an internal “risk score.” The risk score is shared with PayWave’s payment processor and used to automatically place a 72-hour hold on “high-risk” transfers.

After a disputed transfer, Marta downloads her data and notices her profile lists a former address in Madrid and shows multiple logins from that area. She emails PayWave contesting the accuracy of the address and related IP/geolocation entries, stating she moved to Valencia two years ago and was traveling abroad during the flagged logins. She requests restriction of processing while PayWave verifies the data, because the risk score is causing repeated transfer holds.

Separately, Marta submits an Art. 21 objection to PayWave’s fraud-profiling under Art. 6(1)(f), arguing the profiling is excessive and harms her ability to pay rent on time. PayWave replies it will “review the objection,” but continues updating her risk score daily and applying holds. PayWave says it can keep storing the data and may process it only as necessary for fraud investigation and potential legal claims, and it will notify Marta before lifting any restriction.

Yes/No Question:
Does Marta have the right under GDPR Article 18 to obtain restriction of PayWave’s processing of her data (beyond mere storage) while PayWave verifies the contested accuracy and/or completes the Art. 21 balancing review?

A mid-sized fintech lender, BrightBridge Finance, offers personal loans through a mobile app in Germany. To assess creditworthiness, BrightBridge processes applicants’ personal data (name, address, salary, employer, bank statements) and pulls a credit report from a bureau. The app also uses a fraud-prevention vendor that scores applications based on device ID, IP address, and past chargeback indicators. BrightBridge relies on “legitimate interests” for the fraud scoring and “performance of a contract” for core underwriting.

Elena, a customer, is declined for a loan and later discovers the credit report BrightBridge stored shows two missed payments that belong to someone with a similar name. She submits documentation from her bank proving she never held the listed account and formally contests the accuracy of the credit data. At the same time, she plans to file a complaint and potential legal claim for discriminatory treatment because the decline also triggered an internal “high risk” flag that prevents her from reapplying for 12 months.

Elena asks BrightBridge not to delete her application record because she needs it as evidence, but she requests that BrightBridge stop using the disputed credit report and “high risk” flag for any decisions, marketing suppression, or sharing with partners until the data is corrected and the basis for the fraud scoring is reviewed. BrightBridge says it will “look into it” but continues to run automated screening on her profile nightly.

Yes/No Question:
Does Elena have the right under GDPR Article 18 to obtain restriction of processing of her disputed and decision-driving data while BrightBridge verifies accuracy and reviews its legitimate interests?

A mid-sized UK online retailer, “NorthBridge Outfitters,” uses a CRM to store customer profiles (name, email, delivery addresses, purchase history, and a “loyalty tier” score). The CRM syncs nightly with a marketing platform that segments customers for targeted emails and with a fraud-prevention vendor that scores orders using address history and chargeback data.  

Emma, a customer, notices her account shows an old address in Manchester as her “primary address,” even though she moved to Leeds eight months ago and updated her details. She contacts support after a recent order was automatically flagged as “high risk,” delayed for manual review, and she received repeated “Manchester store pickup” promotions. Emma believes the incorrect address is causing both the fraud score and marketing segmentation to be wrong.  

She submits a formal request contesting the accuracy of her address data and asks NorthBridge to **restrict processing** of her personal data while they verify and correct it. She specifically requests that her data not be used for marketing segmentation or automated fraud scoring during the investigation, but she agrees the company may still process what is strictly necessary to fulfill her current order and comply with accounting/tax retention obligations. NorthBridge estimates verification will take 10 business days because it must check audit logs, third-party sync records, and recent delivery confirmations.

Yes/No Question:  
Must NorthBridge restrict processing of Emma’s personal data (e.g., marketing segmentation and automated fraud scoring) while it verifies the contested address accuracy under GDPR Article 18?

BrightHire Ltd. is a UK-based recruitment platform used by mid-sized employers. Maria, a software engineer in Spain, created an account and applied to three roles. BrightHire processes her personal data (name, email, phone, CV, work history, salary expectations, and interview notes) and enriches her profile using an automated “seniority score” derived from public GitHub and LinkedIn data. The platform shares her profile with prospective employers and uses the score to rank candidates in employer searches.

Maria notices that her profile lists her as having “8 years professional experience” and a “low seniority score,” but she has 12 years’ experience. She believes the incorrect experience figure came from an outdated LinkedIn entry BrightHire scraped. After being rejected quickly by two employers, she contacts BrightHire, contests the accuracy of the experience data, and asks that BrightHire stop using her profile for ranking and stop sharing it with employers until the experience figure is corrected. She does not ask for deletion because she still wants to apply for roles once the record is fixed.

BrightHire replies that it can “review the data within 30 days,” but in the meantime it will continue to display her profile in searches and send it to employers because “processing is necessary for the service.” Maria reiterates that she is contesting accuracy and requests restriction of processing while verification is pending.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 18, must BrightHire restrict processing of Maria’s personal data (e.g., ranking and sharing with employers) while it verifies the contested accuracy of her experience information?

NovaPay (an EU fintech) offers “PayLater” instalment loans. It processes customers’ identity data, contact details, transaction history, repayment status, and an internal “delinquency risk score.” NovaPay shares repayment status with two credit reference agencies (CRAs) and uses a third-party analytics provider to run models under a legitimate-interest basis for fraud and default prevention.

Maria notices her NovaPay app shows she is “60 days past due” on a €420 loan she says she repaid in full two weeks earlier. She emails support with a bank transfer receipt and **formally contests the accuracy** of the delinquency flag and risk score. In the same message, she **requests restriction of processing** until NovaPay verifies the data. While the investigation is ongoing, NovaPay’s automated system continues to (i) update Maria’s risk score daily, (ii) send delinquency data to CRAs, and (iii) trigger collections emails.

NovaPay opens a case to verify the payment with its payment processor; it estimates this will take 10 business days. During this period, NovaPay can still **store** Maria’s data but should limit further use. NovaPay considers whether it may continue limited processing to **establish or defend legal claims** if the repayment is disputed. It also notes that once restriction is lifted, it must **inform Maria beforehand**, and—if feasible—**notify the CRAs** that the data was restricted.

Yes/No Question:
While NovaPay verifies whether Maria’s delinquency status is accurate, must it restrict processing (i.e., limit it essentially to storage and permitted exceptions) instead of continuing scoring, collections triggers, and CRA reporting?

MetroCredit, a consumer credit bureau in Spain, maintains files on individuals and provides credit reports to banks and telecoms. After a platform migration, Lina García notices her online file shows two missed loan payments and a “collections” status. She has bank statements showing both payments cleared on time. The file also lists a new email address and phone number she never provided; MetroCredit’s log shows the change came from a bulk “data enrichment” feed purchased from a marketing data broker.

Because of the missed-payment flag, MetroCredit has already sent Lina automated payment-demand emails to the (incorrect) new address and has queued an update to be shared in nightly batch exports with three recipient banks and one telecom. MetroCredit says it will “look into it within 30 days,” but continues routine processing: scoring, disclosure in credit reports, and outbound collections notices.

Lina submits a written request: she contests the accuracy of the missed-payment and contact data and asks MetroCredit to *restrict processing* while it verifies the information—specifically, to stop disclosing the disputed items in reports and to pause collections communications, allowing only storage and internal verification. She also asks MetroCredit to ensure that, if the restriction is later lifted, any recipients who received the disputed data are informed of the change.

Yes/No Question:
Must MetroCredit restrict processing of Lina’s disputed personal data while verifying its accuracy (i.e., limit use/disclosure beyond storage and verification)?

BrightCart, an EU-based online retailer, uses a CRM and marketing automation platform to manage customer accounts, deliveries, and promotions. Lina, a customer in Spain, notices that her account profile shows an old address and a phone number that is not hers. She emails BrightCart contesting the accuracy of these details and explains that recent parcels were misdelivered. BrightCart replies that it will “look into it,” but in the meantime the CRM continues syncing the disputed address and phone number to its courier integration and to its marketing tool, which triggers SMS delivery updates and promotional texts.

Lina then submits a formal request asking BrightCart to restrict processing of her personal data related to the disputed contact details until the accuracy is verified. She asks that BrightCart stop using the contested address/phone for shipping, notifications, and marketing, but she agrees BrightCart may store the data and use her correct email address to communicate about the investigation. BrightCart’s support team can technically flag a record as “restricted,” which pauses outbound syncs and marketing sends while retaining the data in the CRM for audit purposes. BrightCart argues it still has a “legitimate interest” in continuing automated processing to avoid delivery delays.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 18, must BrightCart restrict processing of Lina’s contested address and phone number while it verifies their accuracy?

A mobile telecom provider, NordTel, bills customers based on call detail records (CDRs) and location-derived network logs. NordTel also shares “delinquent account” flags with a contracted debt-collection agency when bills remain unpaid for 30 days. Marta, a customer, receives a final notice stating she owes €312 for international calls placed over two nights while she was abroad on a work trip. In the customer portal, she sees a list of the disputed calls (timestamps, destination numbers, roaming cell IDs) and a “delinquent—send to collections on Friday” status.

Marta believes the CDRs are wrong because her phone was stolen during that period and she reported the theft to NordTel the next morning. She emails NordTel’s privacy inbox, attaches the police report, and explicitly contests the accuracy of the CDRs linked to the €312 charge. She asks NordTel to restrict processing of the disputed CDRs and any related “delinquent” flag while NordTel verifies whether the calls were actually made from her SIM after the theft report. She also asks NordTel not to transmit her account to the debt-collection agency during the verification period. NordTel replies that billing will continue automatically unless she pays first, and the collections transfer is still scheduled.

Yes/No Question:  
Under GDPR Article 18(1)(a), because Marta has contested the accuracy of the personal data, must NordTel restrict processing of the disputed CDRs (and related delinquency status) for the period needed to verify their accuracy?

Maria lives in Spain and has used “FitTrack,” a subscription fitness app, for three years. FitTrack processes her personal data to provide training plans and analytics: profile details (name, email, age, height, weight), workout logs (dates, exercise types, duration, heart-rate zones imported from her smartwatch), GPS running routes, and nutrition entries she manually records. FitTrack stores this data in its cloud database and uses it to generate progress charts and personalized recommendations. Maria pays monthly by card; FitTrack also keeps invoices and transaction references for accounting.

Maria decides to switch to a competing service, “HealthPulse,” which offers better coaching. HealthPulse supports importing user history via a standardized JSON/CSV upload and also offers an API endpoint for direct transfer from other apps. Maria submits a request through FitTrack’s privacy portal asking to (1) receive all personal data she provided and that was observed from her use of the service in a machine-readable format, and (2) have FitTrack transmit the same dataset directly to HealthPulse via HealthPulse’s API, providing her authorization token.

FitTrack replies that it can only provide PDF summaries of her weekly activity and refuses direct transfer, stating that exporting raw workout logs and GPS routes would reveal “proprietary analytics” and that direct transmission is “not supported,” even though FitTrack already has an internal export tool used by its support team.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 20, must FitTrack provide Maria’s data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and, where technically feasible, transmit it directly to HealthPulse without hindrance?

Elena lives in Milan and uses “PulsePath,” a paid fitness app. She signs up for a monthly subscription (contract) and also consents to optional GPS tracking and heart‑rate integration from her smartwatch. PulsePath processes her data entirely by automated means: it collects the profile details she enters (name, email, age, height, weight), her workout entries, and “observed” data such as step counts, heart‑rate time series, GPS routes, and timestamps. The app also generates “derived” outputs like a weekly fitness score, predicted injury risk, and personalized training plans based on proprietary algorithms.

After switching to a competing service, “RunBetter,” Elena uses PulsePath’s in‑app privacy form to request data portability. She asks to (1) receive her personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine‑readable format (e.g., CSV/JSON) and (2) have PulsePath transmit the same dataset directly to RunBetter via an API endpoint RunBetter provides. She specifies she wants the data she provided or that was observed from her use (profile fields, workout logs, step counts, heart‑rate data, GPS routes), but she also asks for the weekly fitness score and injury‑risk predictions.

PulsePath replies it can export a PDF report only, refuses direct transfer “as a policy,” and says it will not include GPS routes because some routes include group runs where other users appear in shared route screenshots, potentially affecting others’ rights.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 20, must PulsePath provide Elena’s portable data in a structured, commonly used, machine‑readable format and, where technically feasible, transmit those data directly to RunBetter at her request (while limiting the scope to data she provided or that was observed and considering others’ rights)?

FitPulse is a subscription fitness app used by Maria in Spain. She pays €9.99/month and accepted the app’s terms to receive personalized training plans (contract basis). FitPulse processes her personal data entirely by automated means: the app collects the profile data she entered (name, email, age, height, weight), her workout logs she manually recorded (exercise type, duration, notes), and “observed” data synced automatically from her smartwatch (step counts, GPS running routes, heart-rate time series). FitPulse also generates “derived” outputs such as a weekly “fitness score,” predicted calorie burn, and injury-risk flags based on its algorithms.

Maria wants to switch to a competing service, TrainBetter. She submits a written request through FitPulse’s privacy portal asking (1) to receive her data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format (e.g., CSV/JSON) and (2) for FitPulse to transmit the same dataset directly to TrainBetter via TrainBetter’s provided API endpoint. She specifies she wants all data “about her,” including raw heart-rate and GPS route history, and also asks for the “fitness score” history.

FitPulse replies that it will only provide a PDF summary unless Maria pays a €25 “export fee,” and refuses direct transfer, saying it is “not supported,” without checking whether its systems can export the requested data or whether the API transfer is technically feasible. FitPulse also notes that some workout notes mention training partners’ names.

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 20, must FitPulse provide Maria the portable dataset (at least the data she provided/that was observed) in a machine-readable format and, if technically feasible, transmit it directly to TrainBetter without hindrance?

PulsePeak GmbH runs a paid fitness app in Germany. Maria (32) subscribes to “PulsePeak Pro” for €9.99/month and accepts a contract and separate consent to connect her Garmin watch. The app processes Maria’s personal data by automated means: account data she provides (name, email, age, height, payment ID), workout entries she types in (runs, notes, perceived exertion), and observed data collected from her watch (heart rate, steps, GPS route, sleep duration) synced automatically. PulsePeak also generates analytics: a proprietary “Fitness Score,” injury-risk predictions, and personalized training plans (inferred/derived data).

PulsePeak proposes emailing a PDF summary instead of providing a machine-readable export and delays the transfer pending “internal review.”

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 20, must PulsePeak provide Maria with a machine-readable copy of the personal data she provided/that was observed and, where technically feasible, transmit it directly to TrainBetter without hindrance (excluding inferred analytics and subject to protecting others’ rights)?

Yes/No Question:
Under GDPR Article 20, must FitPulse provide Marta her provided/observed data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and, where technically feasible, transmit it directly to PeakTrack without hindrance?

Sofia uses “PulsePath,” a paid fitness-tracking app, under a monthly subscription contract. Under GDPR Article 20, must PulsePro provide Marta with her portable data (provided/observed) in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and, where technically feasible, transmit it directly to RunBetter upon her request?

Under GDPR Article 20, must PulsePro provide Marta with her portable personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and, where technically feasible, transmit those data directly to RunSphere at her request (without hindrance)?
